paras: The lynching of Jim Connors took place at Espanola, New Mexico Territory, in June 1881, when masked men took Connors, accused with Harry Knowles of shooting a storekeeper in an attempted robbery, from his guards at night and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Knowles had already been shot dead by a citizens' party pursuing the pair. A wire report carried the episode across the country as the swift punishment of New Mexico "desperadoes", and no article in the coverage gives the race of either man.

Espanola was then the terminus of the Denver & Rio Grande railway, where a large force of graders was at work. According to the Las Vegas Gazette, Knowles had been a clerk in the store of the grocer Goodrich until his discharge a week or more earlier, and he and Connors had been walking about town armed with six-shooters. Goodrich, of the firm of Goodrich, Cherry & Co., had come from Colorado Springs that March, a later letter said.

On Tuesday evening, with Goodrich alone in his store, the two men came onto the platform in front and, by the Espanola correspondent's account, Connors fired without warning. Goodrich was struck, threw a chair at his attacker and fired back, and the two men fled. The first wire reported the proprietor shot twice, "probably fatally," but the local letter described a painful wound that was not dangerous and said he was recovering.

Men who heard of the shooting formed what the Gazette called a "lynching committee," and the correspondent wrote that the whole town turned out to search. Pursuers sighted Knowles up the railroad track near the water tank in the light of a locomotive headlight; he fired, and they shot him dead. Connors hid that night, and the next morning an Indian tracker followed him several miles up the railroad, where he was found asleep, arrested and brought back.

A wire dated June 8 said Connors had been returned that day and "will undoubtedly be lynched tonight." A Santa Fe dispatch of June 11 reported that at midnight six masked men took him from his place of confinement and hanged him from a telegraph pole, where he was found dead in the morning. The Espanola letter said only that he was "taken from the guards and hung" during the night.

"The lynchers are not known," the Santa Fe dispatch stated, and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage. The Espanola correspondent wrote that no one could be identified as taking part but that the town's "reputable men" endorsed the hanging and held that Connors "got his just deserts."

The Denver Tribune's Espanola special was the main channel of national coverage, appearing on June 9 in the Chicago Tribune, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Salt Lake Herald and later in Savannah, Pennsylvania, Montana and New Hampshire papers. Its headlines, among them "Desperadoes Promptly Punished," "New Mexican Outlaws Punished" and "Swift Vengeance," treated the coming lynching as a matter of course. The Chicago Tribune ran it amid a column of crime briefs, beside an Arkansas report of three Black men hanged for murder.

Weekly news summaries shortened the story to a line, the Watertown Republican saying the lynching party shot Knowles "and lynching Conners" and a Mississippi paper that the two were "summarily dealt with by the vigilantes." A Vermont brief reported only that one man was shot and one captured. The Santa Fe dispatch predicted that the two deaths would have "a salutary effect on the rough element in Espanola."

According to the Espanola correspondent, the Santa Fe New Mexican had called the hanging the act of "a lawless crowd," a view the correspondent rejected; the New Mexican's own report was not found. Dates also differ: the wire and the local letter place the hanging on the night after the capture, about June 8, while the Santa Fe dispatch of June 11 puts the shooting on June 9 and the hanging on June 10. The wire named the storekeeper Voorhees, while the territorial papers and the Santa Fe dispatch named him Goodrich.
